title: The sun in my right hand
hookLine: the sirah tells of his answer to Quraysh's offers: even if they put the sun in one hand and the moon in the other, he would not stop

cards: What would it take? That's the question the leaders of Quraysh start asking once the message is public. The sirah says they try offers: money, if he wants money; honor, if he wants honor; leadership, a crown even.
And if it's some sickness, they'll pay for a healer. It's a generous list. They also try pressure, on the man who protects him: his uncle.

teach.b: This story comes to us through the sirah, from Ibn Ishaq. The elders of Quraysh go to Abu Talib and press him: stop your nephew, or step aside and let us deal with him. Abu Talib is shaken.
He calls the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and in effect says: spare me, and spare yourself; don't put on me more than I can carry. And the nephew answers with the line that names today.

As Ibn Ishaq tells it: O my uncle, by Allah, if they put the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left, on condition that I give this up, I would not give it up until Allah makes it prevail or I die in the attempt.
Then, Ibn Ishaq says, he wept, and got up to leave. Not gold, not a kingdom: the sun and the moon. The offer isn't refused because it's too small.

teach.h: NOT FOR SALE AT ANY SIZE.
teach.b: It's refused because the thing he carries isn't for sale at any size.

The sirah keeps another version of the offers too, where a Qurayshi leader named Utbah comes himself with the list, and the Prophet answers by reciting from the Qur'an, from the surah later called Fussilat, until Utbah goes back to his people looking changed.

teach.h: THE SUN IN MY RIGHT HAND.
teach.b: And notice the tears. This is not a hard man enjoying a refusal; it costs him to say no to his uncle. What Abu Talib says next is tomorrow.

how: Muslims retell the sun-and-moon answer in sermons and sirah classes as a picture of steadfastness under pressure; scholars of hadith discuss how strongly the report is transmitted.

games.why: Ibn Ishaq has him say he would not stop even for the sun in his right hand and the moon in his left. then he wept.

practice: Ask yourself what's offered to you, small or large, to let go of something you care about: a shortcut at work, a little gossip to fit in, comfort in place of honesty.
Hold your hands open on your lap, palms up, feel the weight of the offer, and then quietly turn your palms down. If you pray, ask Allah for steadiness.
